description: A build log for C3PO, the Protocol Institute's research assistant — how the corpus was assembled, what decisions were made, and where things stand. Written for readers curious about the process and for future maintainers.

tracks.corpus-ingestion: Assembling and cleaning source material; export parsing, API fetches, enrichment
tracks.vector-architecture: Embedding strategy, chunk design, Pinecone index structure, retrieval quality
tracks.worker-api: Cloudflare Worker API, query routing, prompt engineering, deployment
tracks.ux: Query interface, search UI, result presentation
tracks.operations: Sync scripts, cron jobs, cost monitoring, incident handling

sessions.label: Session 55
sessions.title: The Workshops Were Indexed All Along — Their Content Was Being Thrown Away

items.title: Asking about the symposium returned three years of archive
items.html:
The programme now answers programme questions. Queried at equal weight alongside ten other namespaces, the symposium lost races it should win: "What workshops are happening at the Protocol Symposium?" ranked a 2025 Substack post above the programme and surfaced 2 of the 5 workshops. A question that names the event is now answered from the symposium namespace alone, with the other namespaces skipped rather than fetched and discarded — which also spends less Pinecone egress.

Three limits keep the rule honest. The trigger is the event being named, not any word the programme happens to contain, so "what did the MRG say about memory?" is untouched. A year other than 2026 cancels scoping — without that, "summarize the 2025 symposium" would have been answered confidently from the wrong event. And an explicit reach for prior work keeps the whole corpus in play, because connecting a talk to the archive is the thing the programme page cannot do.

Retrieval is still never filtered by date. A talk that has already been delivered is perfectly good material; time-awareness shapes recommendations, not what can be found.

items.title: During the event, nobody says "symposium"
items.html:
Scoping on the word alone left the questions people actually type during a conference unscoped. "Which sessions run on September 23?" returned 3 of 8 sources from the programme — and three of the rest from C3PO's own build log.

A programme word plus a temporal cue aimed at the event now counts as naming it: an explicit event date at any time, or a relative day (today, tomorrow, this week) only while the event is running. Outside that window "today" says nothing about the symposium, and a programme word with no temporal cue — "what sessions has the MRG held?" — stays unscoped even mid-event.

items.title: A 1,600-character cap was quietly deleting a third of the corpus it touched
items.html:
The workshops were indexed the whole time. What was missing was their content. Each chunk stores the text the model reads separately from the text it was embedded from, and the stored copy was capped at 1,600 characters. So a workshop was retrieved correctly and then described without its takeaways or activities — which, from the outside, is indistinguishable from not being in the index at all.

Measured before the fix: 13,124 characters dropped across the programme, cutting 26 of 61 session chunks and 3 of 5 workshop details mid-sentence. The two richest workshops lost more than half their detail. The slide decks were worse — the chunker targets about 2,300 characters, so 37 of 40 sampled deck chunks sat exactly at the cap, meaning roughly a third of every deck never reached the model. The cap is now 6,000 with a paragraph-boundary trim and a warning above it.

The general shape is worth naming: a limit that only affects what a model sees, never what it finds, produces a system that retrieves the right document and then talks about it badly. Nothing in retrieval metrics would show it.

items.title: Some documents are pointers, and one hop out is the whole answer
items.html:
Three entries in the symposium's Drive folder were not documents. A Drive shortcut pointed at another file in the same folder that was already ingested — the right response being not to ingest it twice. A zip turned out to be a bundle: two slide variants, an HTML export, a framework document and 46KB of speaker notes. And a deck logged for days as an empty stub, "speaker has not filled it in", had exactly one slide reading "Link to slides: …" — the deck was never missing, it was hosted elsewhere. One hop retrieves 14,411 characters of it.

Pointers are followed exactly one hop and only from documents under 400 characters. In a real deck a URL is a citation, and chasing citations would walk the ingest into the open web.

items.title: Seven copies of one workshop, and the rule for collapsing them
items.html:
The AI Kitcraft material existed in seven near-identical forms at 0.70–0.91 token overlap. Ingesting them all would have put roughly 230,000 characters of a single workshop into a namespace where other talks hold two to six chunks each, and duplicate chunks compete for the same retrieval slots.

Files that land on the same talk now collapse to the richest, with the rest recorded and the verdict remembered so a settled group is not re-downloaded every cycle. The threshold is set deliberately low enough to preserve genuinely different documents filed under one talk: a deck and its companion paper score below it and both survive.

items.title: The public build log had started dropping its own history
items.html:
The devlog page renders into a single SQL statement, and D1 caps a statement at 100KB — so the renderer had been truncating from the front. 22 of 56 sessions were missing from the published page.

The row itself can hold 2MB, so the page is now written as one insert plus a series of appends, each sized against a byte budget, and read back and compared before the write is recorded as successful. The log is also paged now — older entries roll into archive files — but that split is invisible: every consumer loads the merged record, so the page, the Markdown rendering and the vector index all still see one continuous history with working anchors.

sessions.label: Session 56
sessions.title: The Symposium, Recorded — Then a Housekeeping Sweep

items.title: Recordings go where the symposium questions look
items.html:
The 2026 Symposium playlist holds 40 recordings, three of them unlisted, so the playlist rather than the channel page is the inventory. They are indexed in the symposium namespace, not with the other YouTube talks. Since session 55, a question that names the event is answered from that namespace alone, so recordings filed elsewhere would have been invisible to exactly the questions that want them.

Each talk gets one summary chunk and a run of transcript chunks. Each transcript chunk carries its start time, and its link opens the video at that moment. Asked what was said about the trust ratchet, C3PO now quotes the talk and links to 7:33.

items.title: A video title names its speaker, so the match has to agree with it
items.html: All 40 recordings are attached to their programme entries. A title match only counts if the speaker named in the video title also appears among the talk's hosts. Without that check, the trial run filed Yuhan Liu's OpenCourier talk under Open Mic: Frontier-Pacing Protocols because both titles contain the word “protocol”. The match was confident and wrong, and an answer built on it would have attributed one speaker's talk to another.

items.title: A deck had been filed under the wrong talk for twelve days
items.html: The post-event pass over the slide folder brought it to 52 files, all matched by reading their contents. One file already in the index turned out to be misfiled: Protocoling had been attached to the Protocol Studies Panel on a weak title match, but its content is Botao Amber Hu's Protocoling HCI. Correcting the attachment exposed a second bug. The sync skipped any file whose bytes had not changed, so moving a deck to a different talk would never have re-embedded it. The talk it belongs to is now part of what “unchanged” means.

items.title: YouTube rate-limits everyone eventually
items.html: YouTube refuses caption requests from the cloud VM, so recording ingest runs from the laptop. Then the laptop got rate-limited as well, after 40 quick caption requests. Switching to a gentler transcript client delivered 19 talks before that was blocked too. The ingest picks up where it stopped, so the other 21 arrive on the next run once the block clears.

items.title: Summaries that read the whole talk
items.html: Video summaries used to be written from the first 3,000 characters of a transcript. At a conference, that is mostly the host introducing the speaker. A symposium recording's summary now comes from the whole talk, with the programme listing's spelling of every name. Auto-captions had produced “Blyger” and worse.

items.title: Intro replies only for new members, now with a video
items.html: C3PO had a “welcome back” reply for anyone who joined more than a week earlier and posted in #introductions. It fired seven times since August and is now gone: only new members get an intro reply. New members also get a Worth watching line. Videos had been 9 of 213 intro recommendations, because a transcript resembles a written self-introduction less than an essay does. The video is chosen from talk summaries. It has to clear a relevance floor, so a forced, off-topic video never appears.

items.title: 97 talks re-read in full
items.html: Every older video's summary had been written by a small model from the first 3,000 characters of an auto-caption: mostly the host's introduction, with names as the captioner heard them. “Benitesh Raalo” was Venkatesh Rao. All 97 were re-summarized from the whole talk, with a list of how community members' names are actually spelled. Given that list too loosely, the model used it to guess who an unnamed presenter was. It now only corrects spelling. The same pass found that the video index stored the first 1,000 characters of each 2,300-character chunk, so most of every transcript was retrieved and then discarded.

items.title: Small things that had been failing quietly
items.html: A daemon checkout of the website repo that had fallen 16 commits behind. Two build-log entries sharing one number, so the log re-embedded one of them every 30 minutes. 28 Discord links recorded as fetched whose vectors never existed, retried every cycle since May. A chat-sync step that died on one dropped connection. SIG pages showing literal ** where bold was meant, reported by the agent that maintains the website. Each is fixed, and checked against the live system rather than assumed.

items.title: Planned: knowing which event something belongs to
items.html: A plan for event and time awareness. C3PO will read the institute's two public calendars and its events history, tag archive items with the event they belong to, and answer questions scoped to any event, generalizing what was built for the 2026 symposium alone.

sessions.label: Session 57
sessions.title: A Reranker, a New SIG, and a Lexicon That Had Lost Its Words

items.title: A reranker, suggested by a community member
items.html:
A member filed issue #10 after a Discord thread on rerankers, with tests run against the open search endpoint. An embedding model turns each passage into a vector before any question exists, which is good at finding the right neighbourhood and coarse at ordering what is in it. A reranker reads the question and each passage together. C3PO now passes its whole candidate pool through Voyage's rerank-3 before choosing the sources an answer is built from, on the web, in Discord and over MCP.

The rerank score is multiplied by the existing source weights rather than replacing them, because those weights say something a reranker cannot know: that the Institute's own papers outrank a passing Discord remark. On “how do protocols die or get replaced”, a Discord post the reranker loved rose from 20th to 8th instead of 2nd. The open search tool gets it as an option (rerank: true), and each result reports its score, so a caller can tell one good match from twenty.

items.title: Five of twenty results were empty
items.html: The issue noted that lexicon terms came back with no text. The cause was worse than it looked: the definitions had never been stored alongside the terms, only used to build their vectors. So every lexicon hit reached the model as a bare word with nothing under it, and still took one of the eight source slots an answer is built from. All 560 definitions were written back in place without re-embedding anything, and items with no text are now dropped before the cut.

items.title: The same passage, at two addresses, at two offsets
items.html: One passage of The Unreasonable Sufficiency of Protocols was indexed twice, once from a gitbook and once from the site that mirrors it. The two copies were chunked at different starting points, so neither the document id nor the opening words matched. Duplicates are now detected by overlapping five-word sequences. On the issue's own query this removes exactly that copy and leaves alone three chunks of one symposium talk.

items.title: Intelligence Media joins the SIGs
items.html: The new Intelligence Media SIG, on Blygger, oracles, bots and extended universes, has no meetings yet, so its Discord channel is ingested as discussion: 8 threads and 325 messages. It is labelled by its full name rather than an abbreviation. When a group's name is shortened, the bot has been known to guess what the letters stand for.

items.title: YouTube is still not answering
items.html: Of the 21 symposium recordings left waiting last session, one came through (Building Psychohistory). YouTube still blocks caption requests from the laptop, so the other twenty wait for another network.

items.title: A new name, and a new front door
items.html: The assistant is now PIBot, at pibot.protocolized.io. The old address still works: a browser opening a page there is sent to the new one, while anything that calls the API or MCP server at the old address is answered as before, because a tool configured against it cannot be assumed to follow a redirect. The MCP tool is now ask_pibot, with the old name kept as a quiet alias.

items.title: What changed, and what deliberately didn't
items.html: The persona, web pages, Terms, How It Works, alerts, Discord copy and handles, the MCP server name, the GitHub repository (Protocol-Institute/pibot) and the Institute's two websites all say PIBot. The plumbing keeps its old names, because renaming it buys nothing anyone can see and risks a lot: the Pinecone index, Worker, queue, VM and its services, environment variables. History is left as written, so the devlog and past conversations still say C3PO.

items.title: The block that wasn't a bug
items.html: Renaming the repository was refused by the session's auto-mode safety classifier, and not retried by another route. Switching the session to manual approval let it through once it was confirmed. Afterwards the VM's repo-scoped tokens were checked the only way that proves anything: by waiting for the daemon's next real push, which landed.

items.title: Knowing what is on the calendar
items.html: PIBot can now answer “when is the next SIGPSY meeting?” and “what was Edge Lanna?” from the Institute’s own calendars rather than from whatever the archive happened to mention. A new sync reads the two public Google calendars and the website’s events history, expands the recurring meetings, and hands the result to the Worker. When a question names an event, or asks when something is, the answer is given a short list of known events to read from; an ordinary question about the content of the archive gets nothing extra. The calendar stays the website’s: PIBot only reads it, and a missing event is fixed there.

items.title: Twice as fast, and words on screen in three seconds
items.html: Answers on the web now stream: the first words appear about three seconds after asking instead of after the whole answer is written, around twenty seconds for a full one. Separately, PIBot moved from Claude Sonnet 4.6 to Claude Sonnet 5.5 after a side-by-side test on ten questions: the same answer length in about half the time (a median of 11 seconds against 23), at the same cost per answer, and on a close reading at least as good, and more willing to say what it does not have. Discord threads now allow eight turns instead of five, matching the web. The test harness that measured all this, and a playbook for applying the same changes to the Institute’s other bots, are in the repository.
